assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a new platform where band structure itself is tunable by a twist angle. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted flat bands from interlayer-tunnelling electronic-structure reasoning, and the 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and gate-tunable superconductivity turned that prediction into a broad field of moire quantum materials. Originality, clarity of the physical idea and the breadth of follow-on work (Chern insulators, nematicity, strange metals) are exceptional, and the theory-experiment pairing is the type of story I find most convincing.
assessment.attribution: A clean three-person configuration is available: the theoretical prediction (Bistritzer, MacDonald) and the first experimental demonstration of correlated and superconducting states (Jarillo-Herrero with his group). Andrei's early STM and transport work on twisted graphene is also significant and the three-person limit forces a hard choice; I regard the prediction plus the 2018 discovery as the decisive core. Credit for the earlier twisted-graphene band-structure work by others is not captured by the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Correlated insulator and superconducting phases have been reproduced by many independent groups across several platforms since 2018, and the continuum-model picture is now standard. The interpretation of the superconducting pairing mechanism is still open, but the discovery itself is robust. Recognition after roughly eight years is timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, though this concerns the follow-up science more than the discovery.
Whether Andrei should displace one of the three proposed laureates is a genuine allocation question that I cannot settle from the supplied credit alone.
Sample-to-sample variability of twist-angle disorder complicates some claims; I rely on my general knowledge here and have not verified details independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall and anomalous Hall effects established that band topology, driven by spin-orbit coupling and in the magnetic case by exchange, yields protected boundary conduction. This is a conceptual change in how we classify electronic phases, with deep links to electronic-structure theory (band inversion in real materials such as HgTe) and to magnetism (quantized anomalous Hall effect in magnetically doped films). Impact on materials discovery has been very large.
assessment.attribution: Kane (theory of the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state), Molenkamp (first experimental quantum spin Hall state in HgTe wells) and Xue (first observation of the quantized anomalous Hall effect) form a coherent trio covering theory, QSH experiment and QAH experiment. The weak points are that Mele (co-author of the Kane-Mele work), Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe prediction) and Hasan (3D topological insulators) are outside this entry's supplied credit, so the fairness of the configuration is debatable and the omissions are real.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups; the QSH state in HgTe and the quantized anomalous Hall effect in magnetic topological insulators are reproduced, and 3D topological insulators are textbook material. Timing is mature, arguably overdue, but the competing credit makes the allocation difficult.
uncertainties: Attribution is contested across several theory and experiment groups; the proposed trio excludes Mele and others who contributed decisively.
Quantization of the QAH effect occurs only at very low temperatures, limiting immediate applications.
The entry combines three related discoveries, which may deserve different recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory provides the first controlled, non-perturbative framework that captures both localized and itinerant behaviour of correlated electrons, giving the Mott transition and quasiparticle physics in one language, and combined with density-functional theory (DFT+DMFT) it is a working tool for real materials. Its influence on the theory of correlated matter is foundational and I know its practical value from direct use in materials modelling.
assessment.attribution: Vollhardt (with Metzner, limit of infinite dimensions), Georges and Kotliar (the mapping onto a self-consistent impurity problem and the Mott transition) are the central figures. Metzner and Vollhardt's infinite-dimension limit is a decisive precursor, and Metzner is not on the supplied list, which leaves a genuine attribution problem; of the supplied names, Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt are the most defensible.
assessment.maturity: The method has existed for over three decades with extensive validation against experiments and exact solutions in model systems. Quantitative predictions for real materials still depend on double-counting and impurity-solver choices, but this does not undermine the formal advance. Timing is mature.
uncertainties: Metzner's role in the infinite-dimension limit is not represented in the supplied credit.
Theoretical Nobel recognition requires a strong experimental link; DFT+DMFT successes are many but individually less decisive than a single confirming experiment.
Conflict of perspective: my own work uses these methods, so I discount my enthusiasm somewhat.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance and the coherent-tunnelling MgO junction are the physics behind modern magnetic read heads and MRAM. The step from small TMR in amorphous barriers to very large TMR in crystalline MgO rests on spin-dependent symmetry filtering of Bloch states, a point where first-principles theory and experiment agreed beautifully. Technological impact is enormous and follows directly from the 2007 spintronics recognition.
assessment.attribution: Moodera (and Miyazaki) established reproducible room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin and Yuasa independently demonstrated large TMR in crystalline MgO in 2004, with theory by Butler and Mathon-Umerski preceding. The supplied list has four names and one must choose three; Miyazaki is a strong alternative to Parkin or Yuasa, and the theory contribution is not credited.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of device deployment and independent confirmation; the physics is fully understood. Timing is arguably late rather than early, though prize committees may view it as an extension of the GMR prize.
uncertainties: Choice among Miyazaki, Moodera, Parkin and Yuasa is delicate and priorities between 1995 and 2004 breakthroughs are disputed.
Theoretical predictions of symmetry filtering are not represented in the credited names.
Possible perception as incremental to the GMR prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and developed by Ye into clocks of extraordinary accuracy and stability, have transformed precision metrology and opened tests of fundamental physics (gravitational redshift at millimetre scales, variation of constants). The idea is original, clear and its impact is lasting, though it sits outside my own area.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice; Ye's group made the leading demonstrations and pushed performance and applications. A two-person prize is natural, but other contributions (for example single-ion clocks, Hall and Hansch comb work already recognized) are acknowledged separately. Credit for related lattice-clock work at other laboratories is not represented here.
assessment.maturity: Multiple laboratories reproduce the clocks and performance continues to improve; the redefinition of the second remains pending. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Ye also appears in other candidate entries, and this entry should be judged independently of that overlap.
My expertise in precision metrology is limited, so I weigh the evidence more cautiously than for condensed matter entries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction that particles in two dimensions can have fractional statistics, and the later measurement of fractional charge and signatures of anyonic exchange in quantum Hall systems, represent a deep conceptual extension of quantum mechanics with direct links to topological order and quantum computing. Originality of the Leinaas-Myrheim analysis is high, and the experiments connect to the physics of correlated two-dimensional electron systems that I follow closely.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim (1977) identified fractional statistics; Heiblum's group provided shot-noise measurements of fractional charge and interferometric experiments, with Fève and Manfra contributing the more recent anyon collider and high-quality-material work. Wilczek's naming and theory, and Laughlin/Halperin/Arovas-Schrieffer-Wilczek theory, lie outside the supplied credit; the fair configuration is therefore uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Fractional charge is confirmed; anyonic braiding statistics has been demonstrated only in recent years (interferometers and colliders) and the interpretation still carries debate about interferometer artefacts. Recognition may be slightly early for the statistics half.
uncertainties: Compound discovery whose parts (theory of anyons, fractional charge, braiding evidence) may merit different recognition.
Wilczek and others are not within the credited names, which weakens the attribution case.
Experimental confirmation of non-Abelian statistics is not claimed here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices implement Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters, enabling the Mott insulator transition and quantum simulation of lattice models, including fermionic Hubbard physics with growing relevance to correlated-electron theory. Impact on many-body physics is considerable and its clarity is high, though prior Nobel recognition of cold-atom physics (2001, 1997, 2012) tempers novelty.
assessment.attribution: Experimental credit centres on Greiner and Bloch (superfluid-Mott transition) and Esslinger (fermionic Mott and band insulators). Theoretical proposals by Jaksch, Zoller and Cirac are decisive precursors and Zoller and Cirac appear in the supplied credit, so a fair allocation between proposal and experiment is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are reproduced widely and quantum gas microscopes have achieved single-site resolution; the field is mature. Whether the simulations yield new solutions to open problems, such as d-wave superconductivity in the Hubbard model, remains unproven.
uncertainties: Theory-versus-experiment allocation among Zoller, Cirac, Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger is unresolved.
Overlap in subject matter with earlier prizes in atomic physics.
Quantum advantage over classical Hubbard simulations is not yet established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a third class of collinear magnetic order with compensated moments yet spin-split bands set by crystal symmetry, a result that elegantly combines symmetry analysis and first-principles electronic-structure calculations and has opened new directions in spintronics. Conceptually it is a real, clean contribution that speaks directly to my own field.
assessment.attribution: The group of Šmejkal, Jungwirth and Sinova formulated the symmetry classification and the spin-group framework; earlier related observations (for example spin-split bands in RuO2 and MnTe predictions from other groups, and unconventional d-wave magnetism by others) complicate the picture. The proposed three share the principal formulation, but allocation relative to earlier and parallel work is not clean.
assessment.maturity: ARPES and other experiments on MnTe and CrSb support the spin-split bands, but the field is only a few years old, several candidate materials (notably RuO2) have disputed magnetic ground states, and technological payoff is not shown. Recognition in 2026 would likely be premature.
uncertainties: Premature: independent confirmation is still maturing and some material claims are contested.
Prior and parallel work on spin-split antiferromagnets could alter credit.
Because it is in my own research area, I may over-weight its promise and so place it lower.
